items.title: The Eightfold Path has three groups: wisdom, conduct, discipline
items.claim: How is the Eightfold Path structured?

options.text: Eight factors in three groups: wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, right action, right livelihood), mental discipline (right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration) — practised together, not sequentially

items.reveal:
The Eightfold Path (ariya atthangika magga) is the content of the Fourth Noble Truth. The three groups (panna/sila/samadhi — wisdom, ethics, mental discipline) reinforce each other.

'Right' (samma) means complete or perfect rather than morally correct in a narrow sense. Right View includes understanding the Four Noble Truths; right intention includes renunciation and non-cruelty.

Right Livelihood excludes specific occupations: trading in weapons, living beings (slavery), meat (butcher), intoxicants, poisons. Right Mindfulness is the practice that secular mindfulness movements have isolated from its Buddhist context.
items.why: The Eightfold Path is not a sequential checklist. The three trainings work together — and modern adaptations (secular mindfulness) often extract one element from a framework designed to be integrated.

items.title: Aquinas offered five arguments for God, not one

options.text: Five distinct arguments from observation: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer) — in Summa Theologiae I.2.3

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes 'a priori' arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from 'a posteriori' arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move and change; an unmoved mover is required to start the chain. Second Way (efficient causation): everything has a cause; a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised individually. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's response to Copleston challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.

items.title: Joseph Fletcher's situation ethics centres on agape
items.claim: What is the central principle of Fletcher's situation ethics?

options.text: There are no moral rules of any kind
The single absolute is agape (selfless love); all other rules are guidelines that can be overridden when love requires it. Set out in 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality' (1966)
Maximise pleasure for the greatest number

items.reveal:
Fletcher's six propositions: (1) Only love is intrinsically good. (2) The ruling norm of Christian decision is love, not law. (3) Love and justice are the same — justice is love distributed. (4) Love wills the neighbour's good. (5) Only the end justifies the means. (6) Love's decisions are made situationally, not prescriptively.

Fletcher gave four working principles: pragmatism, relativism, positivism, personalism.

The Vatican condemned situation ethics under Pius XII (1956, before Fletcher's book) and again in the 1990s. Critics argue that 'love' as the only criterion is too vague to guide decisions; defenders argue agape has specific content (the New Testament's understanding) that excludes self-interested 'love'.
items.why: Christian ethics in the mid-20th century split between absolutist and contextual approaches. Fletcher's situation ethics is a high-profile example of context-driven ethics — challenging the natural law tradition from within Christianity.
